topic.subject: science
topic.title: Electric current and its effects
topic.scope: heating effect, fuse, magnetic effect, electromagnet, electric bell, circuit symbols

misconceptions.statement: A battery provides current to the circuit, and the wire just acts as a path for the current to travel.
misconceptions.why: Students often view the battery as the sole source of electricity and ignore the closed-loop requirement.
misconceptions.fix: Current only flows when there is a complete, unbroken path from one terminal of the battery to the other.

probe.question: If you connect a bulb to only one terminal of a battery, will it light up?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the battery provides the electricity.

misconceptions.statement: Electricity is used up as it flows through a bulb.
misconceptions.why: The word 'consumption' in everyday language leads students to think current is a fuel that gets exhausted.
misconceptions.fix: Current is a flow of charge; the same amount of current that enters a bulb leaves it, but energy is transformed into light and heat.

probe.question: Is the current flowing out of a bulb less than the current flowing into it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the bulb uses up some of the current.

misconceptions.statement: Only high-power appliances like heaters get hot, while wires and bulbs do not.
misconceptions.why: Students only notice heat when it is the intended function of the device.
misconceptions.fix: All conductors offer some resistance to current, which causes them to heat up, though it may be too small to notice in thin wires.

probe.question: Does a connecting wire get warm when a bulb is lit?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only the heater coil gets warm.

misconceptions.statement: A fuse is a device that stores extra electricity to prevent a power surge.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the fuse with a battery or a capacitor due to the term 'safety device'.
misconceptions.fix: A fuse is a thin wire that melts and breaks the circuit when too much current flows, preventing damage.

probe.question: What happens to the fuse when there is a short circuit?
probe.wrong_answer: It releases extra electricity to keep the circuit running.

misconceptions.statement: An electromagnet is a permanent magnet that is powered by electricity.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that because it is called a 'magnet', it must always have magnetic properties.
misconceptions.fix: An electromagnet is only magnetic when current is flowing through the coil wrapped around the core.

probe.question: What happens to an electromagnet when you switch off the current?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays a magnet but becomes weaker.
